title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Brief at a glance
The official exercise brief requires six connected tasks:

Acquire, inspect, clean, validate, transform, and document the spatial data.
Analyse first-order spatial and temporal intensity with justified parameters.
Test second-order spatial structure against a stated null model.
Integrate the first- and second-order evidence, including uncertainty and alternative explanations.
Present readable statistical graphics and maps, with no more than 150 words for each major visualisation.
Write public-safety implications in no more than 500 words, separating evidence from recommendations that need more information.

The bonus analysis must answer a useful geospatial question beyond the core requirements. A new package or decorative visualisation alone does not meet the bonus standard.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Selected study design
The analysis uses Option B: Thailand road accidents in 2022. Event records come from the Thailand Road Accident 2019-2022 dataset, while provincial boundaries come from geoBoundaries Thailand ADM1.
The Bangkok Metropolitan Region is operationalised as Bangkok, Samut Prakan, Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani, Nakhon Pathom, and Samut Sakhon. This six-province definition is documented by Thailand’s National Statistical Office. Distance and area calculations use WGS 84 / UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647).

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Analytical coverage

The data audit traces 81,735 raw records to 3,597 analysed events and documents missing coordinates, spatial filtering, province mismatches and duplicate handling.
First-order analysis compares monthly and hourly patterns, provincial event density and edge-corrected KDE at 2 km, 3 km and 6 km bandwidths.
Second-order analysis uses transformed L-functions, translation edge correction and 99 conditional simulations under CSR and an inhomogeneous Poisson model.
Sensitivity checks compare KDE bandwidths and repeat the inhomogeneous test after removing repeated coordinates.
The bonus applies a 199-run Monte Carlo Knox test at three space-time thresholds.
Fixed URLs, source-file checksums, scripts, parameters, a simulation seed and session information document the workflow.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Geoprocessing

Question 1: How much land is within 5 m of a cycling path?
A five-metre buffer is created on both sides of every cycling-path feature. Summing the separate buffer areas double-counts overlaps, so I also dissolve the buffers with st_union() to obtain the unique footprint.


Show the R code
buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(cyclingpath, dist = 5, nQuadSegs = 30)

naive_buffer_ha <- st_area(buffer_cycling) |>
  sum() |>
  set_units("ha")

dissolved_buffer_ha <- buffer_cycling |>
  st_union() |>
  st_area() |>
  set_units("ha")

overlap_pct <- as.numeric(
  (naive_buffer_ha - dissolved_buffer_ha) / naive_buffer_ha * 100
)

buffer_results <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Sum of individual buffers", "Dissolved unique footprint"),
  `Area (hectares)` = round(c(as.numeric(naive_buffer_ha), as.numeric(dissolved_buffer_ha)), 2),
  check.names = FALSE
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Key findings

The current official spatial files contain 323 subzones, 8,523 cycling-path features, and 2,290 pre-school locations.
Transforming from WGS84 to EPSG:3414 is essential before calculating metres or square kilometres.
The unique five-metre cycling-path buffer covers about 431.51 hectares.
TAMPINES EAST has the most pre-schools (72), while CECIL has the highest density (35.6 per km²).
Count and density answer different questions, and density is sensitive to very small subzone areas.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Limitations
The datasets come from different reference dates, so the analysis is a methodological exercise rather than a fully time-aligned planning study. A five-metre buffer measures geometric proximity, not construction feasibility or legal land acquisition. Density per land area also does not account for the number or age of children living in each subzone.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5

Data and observation windows
The analysis reuses the ECDA Child Care Services points and URA Master Plan 2019 Planning Area Boundary from Exercise 4. All coordinates are transformed to EPSG:3414 so distance is measured in metres.


Show the R code
planning_area <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "MP2019_PlanningArea.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_make_valid() |>
  st_transform(3414)

childcare <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "ChildCareServices.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_transform(3414)

    x = xy[, 1],
    y = xy[, 2],
    window = as.owin(st_union(boundary)),

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
What the four functions test

G-function: nearest-neighbour distances from events; an observed curve above CSR suggests unusually short event-to-event distances.
F-function: distances from empty locations to the nearest event; an observed curve below CSR suggests larger gaps between clusters.
K-function: cumulative event interaction over distance; values above CSR suggest clustering.
L-function: a variance-stabilised transformation of K; values above CSR again suggest clustering.

For each statistic, 99 CSR simulations create a pointwise simulation envelope. The seed makes the exercise reproducible. This is a concise exploratory test; a confirmatory analysis should use more simulations and a global envelope.


Show the R code
set.seed(608)
nsim <- 99

make_envelopes <- function(x) {
  list(
    G = envelope(x, Gest, nsim = nsim, correction = "best", rank = 1, verbose = FALSE),
    F = envelope(x, Fest, nsim = nsim, correction = "best", rank = 1, verbose = FALSE),
    K = envelope(x, Kest, nsim = nsim, correction = "iso", rank = 1, verbose = FALSE),
    L = envelope(x, Lest, nsim = nsim, correction = "iso", rank = 1, verbose = FALSE)
  )
}

envelopes <- lapply(patterns, make_envelopes)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
Compact numerical diagnostic
The table summarises the share of evaluated radii in the clustering direction outside the pointwise CSR envelope. It is a descriptive aid, not a separate p-value.


Show the R code
summarise_envelope <- function(e, direction) {
  valid <- e$r > 0 & is.finite(e$obs) & is.finite(e$lo) & is.finite(e$hi)
  departure <- if (direction == "above") e$obs[valid] > e$hi[valid] else e$obs[valid] < e$lo[valid]
  data.frame(
    `Radii outside envelope (%)` = round(mean(departure) * 100, 1),
    `First departure (m)` = if (any(departure)) round(min(e$r[valid][departure])) else NA_real_,
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

diagnostic_rows <- list()
for (area_name in names(envelopes)) {
  for (statistic in c("G", "F", "K", "L")) {
    direction <- if (statistic == "F") "below" else "above"
    diagnostic_rows[[length(diagnostic_rows) + 1]] <- cbind(
      data.frame(`Planning area` = area_name, Function = statistic, Direction = direction, check.names = FALSE),
      summarise_envelope(envelopes[[area_name]][[statistic]], direction)
    )
  }
}

diagnostics <- bind_rows(diagnostic_rows)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
Answer and limitations
Both planning areas reject the visual expectation of CSR over meaningful distance ranges, with markedly stronger and more consistent clustering in Tampines. G and F describe the nearest-event and empty-space components, while K and L show that the departure persists across broader distances.
The reference process is deliberately simple. Childcare services respond to population and urban form, so CSR is a baseline rather than a realistic causal model. Results also depend on the planning-area boundary, edge correction, duplicate-location handling, and the number of simulations.

The null hypothesis is CSR. Values of the Clark–Evans ratio (R<1) indicate shorter nearest-neighbour distances than expected under CSR; (R>1) indicates a more regular pattern. The CDF edge correction is suitable for the non-rectangular Singapore window.


Show the R code

  childcare_ppp,
  correction = "cdf",
  alternative = "clustered"
)

  Area = "Singapore",
  `Clark-Evans R` = round(unname(ce_sg$statistic), 3),
  `p-value` = format.pval(ce_sg$p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001),
  Decision = ifelse(ce_sg$p.value < 0.05, "Reject CSR", "Do not reject CSR"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text:
Kernel density estimation
bw.diggle() selects a data-driven fixed bandwidth. An adaptive KDE is also estimated: it uses narrower kernels where points are dense and wider kernels in sparse areas. Both surfaces are expressed as estimated centres per square kilometre.


Show the R code
fixed_bandwidth <- bw.diggle(childcare_ppp)

fixed_kde <- density(
  childcare_ppp,
  sigma = fixed_bandwidth,
  edge = TRUE,
  dimyx = 180
)

adaptive_kde <- adaptive.density(
  childcare_ppp,
  f = 0.15,
  edge = TRUE,
  dimyx = 180
)

fixed_grid <- as.data.frame(fixed_kde) |>
  mutate(value = value * 1e6, Method = paste0("Fixed KDE (h = ", round(fixed_bandwidth), " m)"))

adaptive_grid <- as.data.frame(adaptive_kde) |>
  mutate(value = value * 1e6, Method = "Adaptive KDE")

kde_grid <- bind_rows(fixed_grid, adaptive_grid)




Show the R code
ggplot(kde_grid, aes(x, y, fill = value)) +
  geom_raster() +
  geom_sf(data = planning_area, fill = NA, color = "white", linewidth = 0.08, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~Method) +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(planning_area), datum = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", trans = "sqrt", na.value = NA) +
  labs(
    fill = "Estimated centres\nper km²",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )





Fixed and adaptive estimates of childcare-centre intensity




Answer. The fixed-bandwidth surface peaks in Sengkang. The fixed surface is easier to compare across the island; the adaptive surface retains sharper local peaks in dense estates and smooths more aggressively in sparse peripheral areas. KDE measures concentration of facilities, not accessibility or demand satisfaction.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
This exercise follows Chapter 2: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R. It joins population attributes to Singapore’s Master Plan 2019 subzones and asks:

Where are dependency ratios relatively high?
How much does the classification method change the visual message?
Which subzones deserve closer inspection?

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
Data and preparation
The map uses the current official downloadable boundaries and the 2020 Census population table. The course notes use a later SingStat file, but the public table below contains the same subzone-by-age structure needed to reproduce the method.



Dataset
Source
Use




Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea)
URA via data.gov.sg
Mapping units


Resident Population by Planning Area/Subzone, Age and Sex, Census 2020
Singapore Department of Statistics via data.gov.sg
Age-group counts





Show the R code
mpsz <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "MP2019_Subzone.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_make_valid()

population <- read.csv(
  file.path(data_path, "aspatial", "resident_population_2020.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE,
  na.strings = "-"
)

numeric_fields <- setdiff(names(population), "Number")
population[numeric_fields] <- lapply(population[numeric_fields], as.numeric)

# Remove national and planning-area totals, leaving one row per subzone.
population <- population |>
  filter(Number != "Total", !grepl(" - Total$", Number)) |>
  mutate(join_key = toupper(trimws(Number)))

young_fields <- c(
  "Total_0_4", "Total_5_9", "Total_10_14", "Total_15_19", "Total_20_24"
)
active_fields <- c(
  "Total_25_29", "Total_30_34", "Total_35_39", "Total_40_44",
  "Total_45_49", "Total_50_54", "Total_55_59", "Total_60_64"
)
aged_fields <- c(
  "Total_65_69", "Total_70_74", "Total_75_79",
  "Total_80_84", "Total_85_89", "Total_90andOver"
)

population <- population |>
  mutate(
    YOUNG = rowSums(across(all_of(young_fields)), na.rm = TRUE),
    ECONOMY_ACTIVE = rowSums(across(all_of(active_fields)), na.rm = TRUE),
    AGED = rowSums(across(all_of(aged_fields)), na.rm = TRUE),
    DEPENDENCY = 100 * (YOUNG + AGED) / ECONOMY_ACTIVE
  )

residential <- mpsz |>
  left_join(population, by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "join_key")) |>
  filter(Total_Total > 0, is.finite(DEPENDENCY))


The dependency ratio is the number of residents aged 0–24 or 65+ per 100 residents aged 25–64. 234 populated subzones have a valid ratio; unpopulated and unmatched planning polygons are excluded from the thematic analysis.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
Classification matters
Equal-interval and quantile classifications answer different visual questions. Equal intervals preserve the numeric scale; quantiles emphasise relative position among subzones.


Show the R code
equal_breaks <- classIntervals(
  residential$DEPENDENCY,
  n = 5,
  style = "equal"
)$brks

quantile_map <- residential |>
  mutate(
    Class_number = as.integer(cut(DEPENDENCY, unique(quantile_breaks), include.lowest = TRUE)),
    Method = "Quantile: similar number of subzones per class"
  )

equal_map <- residential |>
  mutate(
    Class_number = as.integer(cut(DEPENDENCY, unique(equal_breaks), include.lowest = TRUE)),
    Method = "Equal interval: same numeric width per class"
  )

comparison_map <- rbind(quantile_map, equal_map)

ggplot(comparison_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = factor(Class_number)), color = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
  facet_wrap(~Method) +
  scale_fill_brewer(
    palette = "YlOrRd",
    drop = FALSE,
    labels = c("1 (lowest)", "2", "3", "4", "5 (highest)")
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(fill = "Within-method class") +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.1, "cm")
  )

The equal-interval map is dominated by the low-population outlier Loyang West. Quantiles provide a more useful comparison among the ordinary residential subzones, while the exact values remain available in the table and interactive map.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
Spatio-temporal kernel density
The chapter uses spattemp.density(). The calculation below implements the same product-kernel idea directly: every monthly slice combines a 12 km Gaussian spatial kernel with a one-month Gaussian temporal kernel. Values are rescaled to 0–1 across all six slices to emphasise changes in the location and strength of concentrations.


Show the R code
province_window <- as.owin(st_union(province))
fire_xy <- st_coordinates(fire_sf)

fire_ppp <- ppp(
  x = fire_xy[, 1],
  y = fire_xy[, 2],
  window = province_window,
  checkdup = FALSE
)

target_months <- 7:12
spatial_bandwidth <- 12000
temporal_bandwidth <- 1

monthly_surfaces <- lapply(target_months, function(target_month) {
  temporal_weight <- dnorm(
    (fires$Month_num - target_month) / temporal_bandwidth
  )

  surface <- density(
    fire_ppp,
    sigma = spatial_bandwidth,
    weights = temporal_weight,
    edge = TRUE,
    dimyx = 110
  )

  as.data.frame(surface) |>
    mutate(Month = factor(month.abb[target_month], levels = month.abb[target_months]))
}) |>
  bind_rows()

monthly_surfaces <- monthly_surfaces |>
  mutate(Relative_intensity = value / max(value, na.rm = TRUE))




Show the R code
ggplot(monthly_surfaces, aes(x, y, fill = Relative_intensity)) +
  geom_raster() +
  geom_sf(data = districts, fill = NA, color = "white", linewidth = 0.15, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~Month, ncol = 3) +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(province), datum = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", limits = c(0, 1), na.value = NA) +

  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

The surfaces show activity building on Bangka Island from July, strengthening across western and southern Bangka in August–September, and reaching its strongest and broadest concentration in Bangka Selatan in October. Intensity falls in November and contracts sharply by December.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
Are space and time independent?
Under space-time independence, randomly reassigning dates to the observed locations should leave the number of near-space/near-time pairs broadly unchanged. I use a transparent permutation test:

a spatial pair is “near” when locations are within 10 km;
a temporal pair is “near” when detections are within seven days;
dates are permuted among fixed locations 199 times.

This tests the same independence question as a space-time K-function while keeping the result concise and directly interpretable.


Show the R code
spatial_distance <- as.matrix(dist(fire_xy))
date_number <- as.integer(fires$acq_date)
upper_pairs <- upper.tri(spatial_distance)
near_in_space <- upper_pairs & spatial_distance <= 10000

count_close_pairs <- function(dates) {
  temporal_distance <- abs(outer(dates, dates, "-"))
  sum(near_in_space & temporal_distance <= 7)
}

observed_pairs <- count_close_pairs(date_number)

set.seed(608)
permuted_pairs <- replicate(
  199,
  count_close_pairs(sample(date_number))
)

permutation_p <- (1 + sum(permuted_pairs >= observed_pairs)) / (length(permuted_pairs) + 1)
pair_ratio <- observed_pairs / mean(permuted_pairs)

test_result <- data.frame(
  `Observed close pairs` = observed_pairs,
  `Mean under permutation` = round(mean(permuted_pairs), 1),
  `Observed / expected` = round(pair_ratio, 2),
  `Monte Carlo p-value` = permutation_p,
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(test_result, caption = "Space-time permutation test: 10 km and 7 days")

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
Answers and limitations
1. Are location and time independent? No. The observed data contain 1831 close space-time pairs, 1.87 times the permutation expectation, with (p=) 0.005. Dates and locations therefore show significant interaction at the chosen 10 km / 7-day scale.
2. Where and when is clustering strongest? The largest annual and monthly concentration occurs in Bangka Selatan, peaking in October. The temporal KDE peaks around 11 October, and the space-time density surfaces show the hotspot expanding from July through October before receding.
NASA FIRMS records satellite detections, not verified fire incidents or burned area. Cloud cover, satellite revisit timing, duplicate detections of one fire, confidence, and the chosen bandwidths all affect the pattern. The analysis identifies space-time concentration; it does not establish ignition causes.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Technical Report
text:
Road accidents occur at specific places and times, making point-pattern methods suitable for studying their distribution. The dataset contains 3,597 distinct accident events recorded in 2022 within a six-province Bangkok Metropolitan Region (BMR). I examine where and when those records concentrate and whether nearby events remain unusually common after allowing for broad variation in intensity.
The unit of analysis is a recorded accident location. Traffic volume, road length, vehicle kilometres travelled, road design and enforcement exposure are unavailable, so the results cannot estimate exposure-adjusted accident risk. Areas with many records may simply carry more traffic or contain more mapped roads.



How did the spatial and temporal intensity of recorded BMR road accidents vary during 2022?
Does the point pattern show interaction beyond broad first-order intensity, and at what distances?
For the bonus analysis, were spatially close accidents also unusually close in time after preserving the observed spatial and temporal margins?




I first audit the source data and construct the study window. I then compare temporal and spatial intensity, test complete spatial randomness (CSR) and an inhomogeneous null model, examine bandwidth sensitivity, and apply a Monte Carlo Knox test for space-time interaction.

2.2 Spatial study window
The BMR is operationalised as Bangkok, Samut Prakan, Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani, Nakhon Pathom and Samut Sakhon. This matches the grouping used by Thailand’s National Statistical Office. The six ADM1 polygons form a 7,604.1 km² observation window.
I transform the boundary and events from WGS 84 to WGS 84 / UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647). This projection covers the complete BMR; distance, area, kernel and second-order calculations are consequently made in metres instead of longitude-latitude degrees.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Technical Report

2.3 Point-event definition
One point represents one reported accident occurrence. The temporal field is incident_datetime; the spatial fields are longitude and latitude. Two pairs of rows had different accident codes but the same incident time, coordinates, agency, route, accident type and casualty totals. I treat each pair as one event and retain the earlier record. Events at identical coordinates remain separate when their timestamps differ because they may represent recurrent accidents at the same recorded location.
Records enter the analysis when they have a valid 2022 incident time, complete coordinates within plausible Thailand bounds, and a point inside the union of the six BMR polygons. Coordinates determine inclusion. Ten records labelled as Ayutthaya, Kanchanaburi or unknown fall inside the BMR boundary and are retained.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Technical Report
text:
5.1 Research question and test design
The second-order question is whether accidents retain more neighbours within 0-15 km than expected after broad intensity variation is represented. I use the transformed L-function, \(L(r)-r\), because zero is the theoretical reference under a Poisson process. Positive departures indicate more neighbours within distance \(r\) than the null predicts; negative departures indicate fewer.
I compare two null models:

CSR: 99 simulations place the observed number of events uniformly within the BMR. It supplies a simple benchmark, although uneven roads and activity make uniform intensity unrealistic.
Inhomogeneous Poisson: 99 simulations draw the observed event count from a fixed 6 km pilot intensity. Broad first-order variation is retained while events remain independent conditional on intensity.

Both tests use 0-15 km at 250 m intervals, translation edge correction, WGS 84 / UTM 47N and pointwise 95% simulation envelopes. A maximum-standardised-deviation statistic supplies a global Monte Carlo test. Conditioning on event count prevents total-count variation from dominating the comparison.

CSR is rejected by the global deviation test (\(p\) = 0.01), and the observed curve lies above the envelope from 0.25 km through 15 km. The comparison confirms that apparent concentration on a map is insufficient evidence without a statistical reference.
The inhomogeneous null is also rejected (\(p\) = 0.01). The observed curve is above the envelope from 0.25 to 14.50 km. The broad first-order trend therefore does not account for all of the excess neighbouring events. The result may also reflect road-network support, shared coordinates or a pilot surface that is too smooth to represent every relevant component of intensity.

title: Where and when did road accidents concentrate?

title: Where and when did road accidents concentrate?
text:
1. Decision question


3,597distinct accident events

Where and when did recorded road accidents concentrate, and did events remain spatially dependent after broad intensity was controlled?

The analysis screens locations and periods for follow-up. It measures recorded events, not traffic-adjusted accident risk.

6. Does the pattern change with bandwidth?


Event-level intensity ranks correlate at 0.97 for 2-3 km and 0.87 for 3-6 km. The metropolitan core is stable; local peak boundaries are not.

section: 7. Do events interact beyond broad intensity?
text:
7. Do events interact beyond broad intensity?


CSR and the inhomogeneous null are both rejected by the global deviation test (\(p=0.01\)). After a 6 km broad-intensity surface is controlled, excess neighbouring events remain from 0.25 to 14.5 km.
Keeping one event per exact coordinate gives the same global result (\(p=0.01\)); repeated coordinates do not explain the remaining structure.

title: Where and when did road accidents concentrate?
text:
9. Planning implications and limits


What the evidence supports


Start detailed diagnostic review in Bangkok and towards Samut Prakan.
Review staffing and monitoring during the October-December rise and evening hours.
Use short-horizon cluster alerts to trigger local investigation.
Follow with road-segment analysis and site inspection before selecting interventions.



What is still needed


Traffic volume or vehicle-kilometre exposure
Verified road-segment locations and road design
Weather, road works and enforcement activity
Audit of shared coordinates and agency coverage




These results identify concentrations of recorded events. They do not establish causation or rank exposure-adjusted road risk.
